paras: The lynching of George Ellis took place in the early hours of June 3, 1882, when masked men took him from the jail at Catlettsburg, Kentucky, and hanged him to a sycamore tree at Ashland. Ellis had been convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to life imprisonment the day before, on an indictment for the killing of three children at Ashland the previous December, after testifying against two co-defendants. The case was carried by wire across the country and drew editorials both excusing and condemning the mob.

In December 1881 a house in Ashland was the scene of what a Catlettsburg correspondent called a "triple crime of rape, murder and arson," with Emma Thomas, Fannie Gibbons and Robbie Gibbons named as the victims. According to the same account, Ellis went voluntarily before a citizens' committee and confessed that he, Ellis Craft and William Neal had committed the crime, claiming he had been forced to take part. Craft and Neal were tried in January, convicted and sentenced to hang, and their appeals were pending before the Court of Appeals.

In January the three prisoners were taken from Catlettsburg under military escort to escape a mob. Ellis was brought back from the Lexington jail for trial, and on Friday, June 2, the jury returned a verdict of manslaughter with a life sentence.

Between one and two o'clock the next morning, disguised men took over the engine house of the "Chataroi" railroad at Ashland, fired up an engine and ran it five miles to Catlettsburg, arriving about three o'clock. The Ashland dispatch put their number at about thirty, the Catlettsburg correspondent at about sixty, and a later summary at 100. Refused admittance, they broke a window in the jailer's residence, took the cell keys by force, and led Ellis out with a halter around his neck.

The train carried him back to Ashland, where he was hanged to a sycamore close to where the Gibbons house had stood, and the men then dispersed. The Maysville Evening Bulletin reported that Ellis repeated his original confession, asked the mob not to mutilate his body with bullets, and declined to pray.

News of the hanging spread quickly, and more than a thousand people visited the body before the coroner arrived about nine o'clock. The coroner's jury found that Ellis "came to his death from the hands of unknown parties," and the correspondent wrote that the mob were so disguised that no one could recognize them. No report of arrests or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage.
Kentucky papers reported that people in the area blamed the Court of Appeals for its delay in the Craft and Neal cases. In Lexington, Craft told a reporter he regretted Ellis's death.

Most papers ran a short Times-Star special sent from Cincinnati, under headlines such as "George Ellis Hanged by a Mob" in the Memphis Appeal and "Justice From Judge Lynch" in the Grant County Herald. Other headlines were harsher toward Ellis: the Omaha Bee printed "A Rapist Roped," and the Stark County Democrat "A Kentucky Brute Taken From Jail and Lynched." Briefs in papers from Raleigh to St. Johnsbury, Vermont, and Abbeville, South Carolina, kept the story in circulation through June 21.

Editorial opinion divided: the Seattle Post-Intelligencer cited the case without names as proof that lenient verdicts drove people to lynch law, writing that "the people could no longer stand it." The Point Pleasant Weekly Register wrote "We regret the deed, and yet the provocation was great," while warning against "midnight mobs." The West Virginia Freeman called the hanging a "popular murder," and the Lancaster Intelligencer called lynching the method of "anarchy, not of government."
None of the coverage mentions the race of Ellis or of anyone else in the case.

The Bourbon News placed the lynching on "Friday night" and the South Kentuckian on "Friday morning," though the verdict came on Friday forenoon and the dated dispatches say early Saturday. Accounts also differ on the train: two flat-cars, four coaches, or a chartered train. The press-association report said the crowd would not let the body be cut down, while the Catlettsburg correspondent wrote that the coroner had it cut down.

bases: A masked group took Ellis from the Catlettsburg jail the night after his conviction and hanged him at Ashland (A4, A23, A25).

A disguised mob reported at 30 to 100 men broke into the jail, took Ellis and hanged him (A23, A25, A27); the papers tied it to the jury's manslaughter verdict and life sentence in the Gibbons murders, which the Catlettsburg letter framed as 'a life for a life' (A23, A14).
The Times-Star special (A4, A21), the National Associated Press report (A9), a Catlettsburg letter (A10, A22/A23) and an Ashland dispatch (A25) agree on the seizure and hanging.

accounts.label: Times-Star special (wire)
accounts.gist: A masked mob came by rail from Ashland at 3 a.m., took Ellis to Ashland near the scene of the Gibbons murders and hanged him to a sycamore; he had been convicted of manslaughter the day before.

accounts.label: National Associated Press
accounts.gist: Masked men chartered a train at Ashland, reached Catlettsburg at 2:30 a.m. Saturday and hanged Ellis at the scene of the murder; the crowd refused to let the body be cut down after the inquest.

accounts.label: Catlettsburg correspondent
accounts.gist: About sixty disguised men seized an engine and two flat-cars, broke into the jail through the jailer's residence, took the keys by force, and hanged Ellis behind the Gibbons premises; the coroner cut the body down about 9 a.m. and the jury found death at the hands of unknown parties.

accounts.label: Ashland dispatch
accounts.gist: About thirty masked men took an engine and four coaches from the Chataroi engine house, had the watchman walk ahead with a lantern, took the keys from the jailer and hanged Ellis near where the Gibbons house had stood.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Times-Star or press-association item under heads such as 'George Ellis Hanged by a Mob', 'A Kentucky Lynching' and 'Justice From Judge Lynch'.
The Omaha Bee headed it 'A Rapist Roped' and the Stark County Democrat 'A Kentucky Brute Taken From Jail and Lynched', and the Catlettsburg letter judged the lynching satisfactory to local citizens.
The Seattle Post-Intelligencer's 'Prevalence of Lynch Law' said the people 'could no longer stand it' after a manslaughter verdict and blamed the courts.
The Point Pleasant Weekly Register wrote 'We regret the deed, and yet the provocation was great' while warning of 'midnight mobs'.
The West Virginia Freeman called it a 'popular murder' with 'no excuse', and the Lancaster Intelligencer called lynching a method of 'anarchy'.
Kentucky papers blamed the Court of Appeals' delay, and the Bourbon News made a joke of the sycamore.

conflicts.note: The verdict came Friday forenoon (A1), so a Friday-morning lynching is impossible; the dated dispatches place it in the early hours of Saturday.
